## ARGUMENT

### A collection letter violates the FDCPA when the least sophisticated debtor could reasonably read it in two or more ways, one of which is inaccurate.

**A. The least-sophisticated-debtor standard protects consumers from ambiguous collection letters.**

Congress enacted the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act "to eliminate abusive debt collection practices," and the statute is remedial, so courts construe it broadly in favor of consumers. *Brown v. Card Serv. Ctr.*, 464 F.3d 450, 453 (3d Cir. 2006); *Caprio v. Healthcare Revenue Recovery Grp., LLC*, 709 F.3d 142, 148 (3d Cir. 2013). Section 1692e bars "any false, deceptive, or misleading representation or means in connection with the collection of any debt," 15 U.S.C. § 1692e, and § 1692e(10) specifically prohibits "any false representation or deceptive means to collect or attempt to collect any debt." Whether a communication is deceptive is judged from the perspective of the "least sophisticated debtor." *Wilson v. Quadramed Corp.*, 225 F.3d 350, 354 (3d Cir. 2000); *Rosenau v. Unifund Corp.*, 539 F.3d 218, 221 (3d Cir. 2008); *Campuzano-Burgos v. Midland Credit Mgmt., Inc.*, 550 F.3d 294, 298 (3d Cir. 2008).

That standard is objective and protective. It safeguards "the gullible as well as the shrewd," and it ensures that collection letters are not decoded only by those with legal training or unusual care. *Brown*, 464 F.3d at 453–54; *Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55. It also has limits. The debtor is presumed to read the letter carefully and to possess a basic level of understanding and willingness to read with care, and bizarre or idiosyncratic interpretations do not count. *Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55; *Rosenau*, 539 F.3d at 221. Within those limits, the standard puts the burden of clarity on the collector, who controls the content of the letter.

**B. A letter is deceptive if it can reasonably be read to have two or more meanings, one of which is inaccurate.**

Applying that standard, this Circuit holds that a collection letter is deceptive when it "can be reasonably read to have two or more different meanings, one of which is inaccurate." *Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354 (quoting *Russell v. Equifax A.R.S.*, 74 F.3d 30, 35 (2d Cir. 1996)); accord *Rosenau*, 539 F.3d at 222; *Caprio*, 709 F.3d at 149. Under this rule, a collector cannot defend a letter by pointing to one accurate reading if another reasonable reading is false or misleading. It is enough that the letter is "reasonably susceptible" to the inaccurate interpretation. *Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55. The plaintiff need not prove that she actually adopted the inaccurate reading, or that the collector intended to deceive. Section 1692e is a strict-liability provision as to intent, and the inquiry is objective. *See Brown*, 464 F.3d at 454; *Lesher v. Law Offices of Mitchell N. Kay, PC*, 650 F.3d 993, 997 (3d Cir. 2011).

The rule follows from the statute's purpose. A debtor who receives an ambiguous letter faces a choice between guessing at its meaning and risking a mistaken response, such as paying a sum not owed or forgoing a right, or seeking legal advice she may be unable to afford. The FDCPA places the cost of that ambiguity on the party that drafted the letter and could easily have clarified it. *See Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55; *Barbato v. Greystone All., LLC*, 916 F.3d 260, 265–66 (3d Cir. 2019).

**C. The ambiguity must concern a material matter.**

This Circuit also requires that the misleading statement be material, meaning it must be capable of influencing the debtor's decision or ability to pay or challenge the debt. *Jensen v. Pressler & Pressler*, 791 F.3d 413, 421 (3d Cir. 2015). This requirement is no obstacle here. Materiality asks whether the inaccurate reading could affect how the least sophisticated debtor responds. It does not require proof that any particular debtor was in fact harmed. *Id.*

**D. Application.**

[Insert record-specific analysis: (1) quote the operative language of Defendant's letter; (2) identify the reading that is accurate; (3) identify the reasonable alternative reading that is inaccurate, and explain why it is not bizarre or idiosyncratic; and (4) explain how the inaccurate reading could affect the debtor's decision to pay, dispute, or seek counsel.]

Because Defendant's letter is reasonably susceptible to at least one inaccurate reading, it violates 15 U.S.C. §§ 1692e and 1692e(10) as a matter of law under *Wilson*, *Rosenau*, and *Caprio*. The district court's contrary conclusion should be reversed.
